payload.body:
You have a way of putting the complicated part into words that other people remember. You ask the question that changes the discussion, notice what an explanation leaves out, or make something understandable enough that other people can finally decide what to do with it.

That ability can become part of your reputation early. A teacher asks you to explain it to the group, people want you to write the message, or a project starts depending on your ability to find the missing fact and make the distinction that matters.

Being the clearest person can also make you responsible for language that is not actually yours. You become the one asked to explain the rule, represent the group, clean up the confusion, or speak for a decision somebody else made.

When your name is attached to the explanation, you need access to the facts and enough authority to correct what is wrong. Being known for clear thinking should give you something you can stand behind, not make you the permanent voice of decisions other people control.
